term_glossary.tooltip: Layers of Cryptographic Keys: an OCP architecture for hardware-rooted storage key protection and lifecycle control.
Self-encrypting drive: a storage device that encrypts media data internally.
Key Management Block: the protected Caliptra component allowed to execute L.O.C.K. operations, read MEKs, and program the encryption engine.
Media Encryption Key: up to 512 bits of key material used by a storage encryption-engine slot to protect media data.
Rendering encrypted data irrecoverable by securely eliminating the key material required to decrypt it.
Device Protection Key: a device-unique root key derived from hardware secrets.
Management Protection Key: an ordered, optional layer used to represent an administrative boundary.
Epoch Protection Key: the active epoch layer formed from a hardware epoch key and software epoch key.
Hardware Epoch Key: one of 4 to 16 256-bit values provisioned in fuse slots.
Software Epoch Key: durable software-controlled epoch material combined with the HEK.
Volatile Encryption Key: a lazily generated key that protects enabled MPKs held in volatile memory.
MEK Derivation Key: a device-unique key used in random-key inner wrapping and derived-MEK generation.
Hybrid Public Key Encryption: the public-key envelope used to establish protected access material.
Special Function Register: a memory-mapped register used for protected MEK transfer and control.
A metadata field identifying the target storage encryption engine.
A metadata field identifying a key slot within the target encryption engine.
Known-answer test: an optional command used to verify MEK transfer behavior against a known result.
The hardware root-of-trust environment hosting the KMB; L.O.C.K. v1.1 targets version 2.1 or newer.

slides.title: OCP L.O.C.K.: Layered Open-source Cryptographic Key Management
slides.subtitle: Trust Boundaries and Security Goals
slides.transcript:
Module one. OCP L.O.C.K. stands for Layered Open-source Cryptographic Key Management. This module focuses on trust boundaries and security goals for data-at-rest keys.

Self-encrypting drives already encrypt user data, but encryption alone doesn't prove that the keys were protected or erased correctly. OCP L.O.C.K. Version 1.1 moves Media Encryption Keys into a protected Caliptra Key Management Block. Drive firmware can request key-lifecycle operations, but it can't read the raw keys.

This module explains the operating problem, the adversary the design assumes, and the trust boundary that makes the design useful. Narration starts automatically. Use the arrow controls, or press Space, when you're ready to advance.

slides.title: A Three-Module Path Through L.O.C.K.
slides.subtitle: Start with the trust model, then follow the keys and integration contract.

figure.alt: Official Google, Microsoft, Samsung Electronics, KIOXIA, and Solidigm contributor logos.

slides.transcript:
This is the first of three modules in the OCP L.O.C.K. Academy course.

Here, you'll learn why operators need more assurance than an erase command issued to ordinary drive firmware. You'll classify the threat model, identify the security guarantees, and trace the protected path through Caliptra.

Module two follows the key hierarchy. It explains how data, multi-party, and epoch protection keys combine around a Media Encryption Key. It also compares soft and hard cryptographic erase and the paths for random and derived media keys.

Module three moves into integration. It covers the mailbox and SFR interfaces, command ordering, reset behavior, and the mandatory controls in version 1.1.

The specification was contributed through OCP by Google, Microsoft, Samsung Electronics, KIOXIA, and Solidigm. Their names and official logos appear here as contributor acknowledgments, not as product endorsements. Together, the three modules are designed for engineers who understand storage and basic cryptography but are new to the L.O.C.K. architecture.

slides.title: Retiring Data Should Not Require Retiring the Drive
slides.subtitle: L.O.C.K. makes the key lifecycle an explicit hardware security boundary.

bullets.text: Organizations may physically destroy usable drives because proving data destruction is difficult.
Cryptographic erase can retire protected data by eliminating the required key material.
A drive can move to another tenant or environment without carrying the prior epoch’s decrypt capability.
L.O.C.K. defines interoperable security behavior for self-encrypting storage controllers.

figure.alt: Animation contrasting physical drive destruction with cryptographic retirement and safe drive reuse.
figure.caption: A key-lifecycle boundary can preserve the hardware while retiring the protected data.

entries.text: Destroy a usable drive because proving the prior tenant's data is unrecoverable is difficult.
Retire the epoch and the parent material needed to recover protected MEKs.
Data retires; hardware can be reused

slides.transcript:
The security problem begins at the end of a drive's first service life.

A storage device leaves its supplier, enters a data center, and accumulates customer data. When the device is retired, the operator must decide whether it can leave the controlled environment. Customer data cannot leave with it. The operator therefore needs high confidence that every usable copy of every Media Encryption Key is gone.

Self-encrypting drives support cryptographic erase. In principle, deleting a media key makes its ciphertext permanently unreadable. In practice, a cloud operator may not trust an erase performed entirely by complex drive firmware. A firmware bug, a compromised signing key, an incomplete key binding, or recoverable key material can turn a successful status code into false assurance.

The conservative answer has been physical destruction. That protects confidentiality, but it also prevents reuse, refurbishment, and component recovery. The result is avoidable electronic waste.

OCP L.O.C.K. creates another branch in that lifecycle. It isolates keys inside a hardware-rooted management block and ties all active media keys to epoch material that can be zeroized and reported. At the 2026 OCP EMEA Summit, the presenters emphasized the operator's goal: reason about the drive in isolation, without proving that every customer, platform, or backup copy of an external key has disappeared.

That doesn't make every failed device recoverable. If a controller is too damaged to perform and report the required zeroization, the same assurance isn't available. But when the protected operation succeeds, cryptographic erase can support reuse instead of automatic destruction.

slides.title: Assume Powerful Attackers—But Separate Security from Availability
slides.subtitle: The guarantees remain meaningful even when ordinary controller software is compromised.

bullets.text: Attackers may control firmware, observe or modify external traffic, or gain physical access to non-protected storage.
Device-unique secrets, the KMB, and the engine key path remain inside the hardware-rooted boundary.
Compromise outside that boundary must not reveal usable MEKs or revive erased key state.
Denial of service, media damage, or refusal to process I/O are not confidentiality failures.

figure.alt: Threat model matrix separating attacker capabilities, protected assets, and availability exclusions.
figure.caption: The model protects key confidentiality and erasure semantics, not uninterrupted service.

entries.text: Denial of service, media damage, or refusal to process I/O can still occur.

slides.transcript:
OCP L.O.C.K. protects user data at rest against an unusually capable adversary. The point of the threat model is not to predict one attack. It is to decide which components may be trusted with a Media Encryption Key.

The adversary may intercept a drive in the supply chain or steal it from a data center. They may open the package and inspect it destructively. They may run arbitrary firmware, even after compromising a vendor's signing keys. They may glitch general-purpose cores or recover key-related clues from debug dumps and UART logs.

The model also assumes that class-wide, global, or shared symmetric secrets can be stolen. A hostile tenant may execute code in a virtual machine on a multi-tenant host that controls the attached device. And the adversary may know every published design document, source file, and RTL description. Openness is not treated as secrecy.

Those capabilities expose five failure classes. Firmware bugs or side channels may leak media keys. Invasive analysis may recover keys that firmware claimed to erase. Credentials may be bound incorrectly. A vulnerable host may expose a valid credential. Or a buggy host may fail to carry out cryptographic erase completely.

Physical denial of service remains out of scope. An attacker standing beside a drive may still destroy it or prevent it from operating. L.O.C.K. is designed to preserve confidentiality and trustworthy key lifecycle behavior, not device availability under every physical attack.

slides.title: Three Guarantees Turn Key Handling into an Architecture
slides.subtitle: Each guarantee constrains both storage and controller implementation.

bullets.text: MEK material must not become readable by ordinary firmware, host software, or external interfaces.
Encrypted media remains unintelligible without the intended hierarchy and active epoch.
Destroyed epoch or parent-key state cannot be reconstructed from residual device information.
Only the KMB may read an MEK and program the storage encryption engine.

figure.alt: Three-part diagram showing key secrecy, data protection, and irreversible key-state retirement.
figure.caption: The protected path connects confidentiality, correct use, and irreversible retirement.

entries.text: Only the KMB can read MEKs and program the engine

slides.transcript:
Three guarantees shape the L.O.C.K. architecture.

First, isolate Media Encryption Keys from ordinary drive firmware. With L.O.C.K. enabled, Caliptra acts as the Key Management Block. The KMB is the only component that can read a raw media key and program it into the encryption engine. Drive firmware still decides when a lifecycle operation should happen, but it invokes a protected service instead of manipulating the key itself.

Second, bind each media key to externally supplied protection material. One Data Protection Key represents the nominal data owner. Zero or more Multi-party Protection Keys can require additional authorities to assent before the media key becomes usable. Those external access keys are injected with replay-resistant HPKE transport, so a remote key service can authorize the device without disclosing its access key to the host.

Third, bind every active media key to an Epoch Protection Key. That composite key depends on both a Soft Epoch Key in rewritable storage and a Hard Epoch Key derived from fuse-held material. Zeroizing either component makes the existing media-key protection chain unrecoverable. The device can report whether the required epoch material is available, supporting an attestable erase state.

These guarantees divide responsibilities. Hardware-rooted Caliptra protects and operates on key material. Drive firmware implements policy, host protocols, and authorization. The vendor encryption engine performs line-rate data encryption. Security comes from keeping those roles separate while defining narrow interfaces between them.

slides.title: Policy Can Cross Firmware; Plaintext MEKs Cannot
slides.subtitle: The KMB is the narrow bridge between lifecycle commands and the encryption engine.

bullets.text: A host or key service requests lifecycle actions through controller APIs.
Ordinary firmware can carry commands and wrapped objects without seeing plaintext MEKs.
Caliptra’s KMB unwraps, derives, loads, zeroizes, and reports key state inside the root of trust.
MEKs move through dedicated secure registers from the KMB to the encryption engine.

figure.alt: Animation showing control messages passing through firmware while MEK material remains inside the KMB-to-encryption-engine protected path.
figure.caption: Commands are observable; plaintext MEK transfer remains inside the protected boundary.

slides.transcript:
The protected path becomes clear when we follow control and key material separately.

The host or a remote Key Management Service starts with an administrative request. It may unlock data, enable a multi-party condition, load a key, or perform cryptographic erase. That request reaches the storage controller and its drive firmware. In Caliptra Subsystem, the firmware runs on the Manufacturer Control Unit, or MCU.

Drive firmware translates the host operation into a mailbox request for the Key Management Block. It can supply a Soft Epoch Key, a Data Protection Key, sealed access keys, enabled MPKs, and vendor-defined metadata. It can also retain encrypted keys. But it never receives a plaintext Media Encryption Key from the KMB.

Inside Caliptra, the KMB unwraps HPKE payloads, derives the required protection chain, and generates, unwraps, or derives the media key. Hardware-protected Key Vault slots hold the most sensitive intermediate values. Other values exist only in protected volatile or ephemeral memory for the operation that needs them.

The final media key moves directly from the KMB into the vendor encryption engine. The engine stores it in a volatile key cache, bound to non-secret metadata that selects the correct namespace, address range, or key tag. User data then passes through the engine for line-rate encryption and decryption.

The critical boundary is simple: firmware controls the request and the metadata, while Caliptra and the encryption engine control the raw media key. That is the architectural answer to the threat model.

slides.title: L.O.C.K. Complements Storage Protocols and Security Frameworks
slides.subtitle: It standardizes internal key protection without forcing a single host protocol.

bullets.text: The architecture is not limited to NVMe and can be integrated into different storage-controller command sets.
It can support TCG Opal, Enterprise, and Key Per I/O management models.
Version 1.1 targets the Caliptra Subsystem 2.1 or newer KMB security services.
The design can align with OCP S.A.F.E.™ while keeping each framework’s scope distinct.

figure.alt: Layer diagram showing L.O.C.K. between host security protocols, Caliptra, and OCP S.A.F.E.™ using their official logos.
figure.caption: L.O.C.K. defines the controller’s key boundary, not a replacement for every surrounding protocol.

entries.text: internal key hierarchy · lifecycle · protected transfer

slides.transcript:
L.O.C.K. is a Caliptra feature set, but its deployment boundary is broader than one drive protocol.

Version 1.1 targets Caliptra Subsystem 2.1 and later. Caliptra ROM, runtime firmware, protected hardware, and a vendor encryption engine form the key path. Host-facing drive firmware exposes the storage protocol outside that boundary.

The design is not restricted to NVMe. It can support self-encrypting storage devices using TCG Opal, Enterprise, or Key Per I/O. It can also support the TCG Media Encryption Key Multiparty Authorization feature. L.O.C.K. therefore strengthens the implementation behind existing storage operations instead of inventing a new host protocol for every product.

Drive firmware still owns important policy. It authorizes destructive lifecycle actions, obtains the Data Protection Key, chooses which MPKs bind to a media key, and maps that key to the correct locking range or cache entry. The KMB protects and executes the key operation; it does not replace the product's authorization model.

Some standards combinations need additional review. For example, one Common Criteria profile can conflict with Key Per I/O when an injected key is conditioned for cryptographic erase.

That is why integration review matters. An OCP S.A.F.E. review can examine the Caliptra boundary and verify that drive firmware invokes these protected services correctly.

slides.title: Trust the Narrow Path, Not the Whole Controller
items: Cryptographic retirement can separate data destruction from drive destruction.
The threat model allows compromised ordinary firmware without surrendering plaintext MEKs.
The KMB is the only component permitted to read MEKs and program the encryption engine.
Availability failures are distinct from confidentiality and irreversible-erasure guarantees.
L.O.C.K. complements existing storage protocols and OCP security frameworks.
slides.transcript:
The L.O.C.K. security model starts with a practical requirement: prove that retired media cannot expose customer data without destroying every drive by default.

It assumes a strong adversary. Stolen hardware, arbitrary firmware, invasive analysis, compromised shared secrets, hostile tenant code, and complete knowledge of the design are all inside the model.

The response is a narrow trust boundary. Caliptra's Key Management Block alone reads Media Encryption Keys and programs the encryption engine. Drive firmware requests operations and supplies policy inputs, but it doesn't handle raw media keys.

Protection comes in layers. A Data Protection Key represents the data owner. Optional Multi-party Protection Keys add other authorities through protected HPKE transport. Hard and Soft Epoch Keys make cryptographic erase an explicit state transition.

L.O.C.K. can support several self-encrypting storage protocols and isn't limited to NVMe. But integration still requires authorization, correct reset handling, and an OCP S.A.F.E. review. The next module opens the key hierarchy and follows each layer through its lifecycle.

You can now explain why cryptographic erase needs a protected trust boundary, what attacker capabilities the design assumes, and why drive firmware must never receive raw media keys.

modules.title: Key Hierarchy and Lifecycle
modules.subtitle: Four layers, three persistence classes, and two MEK strategies.

slides.title: OCP L.O.C.K.
slides.subtitle: Key Hierarchy and Lifecycle
slides.transcript:
Module two. OCP L.O.C.K. key hierarchy and cryptographic erase.

The trust boundary from module one becomes useful only when every Media Encryption Key depends on the right protection layers. A Data Protection Key represents the owner. Optional Multi-party Protection Keys add other authorities. Hard and Soft Epoch Keys make erase a change in cryptographic state. An MDK constrains the final hardware path.

This module follows those keys through generation, storage, enablement, rotation, and zeroization. By the end, you'll be able to reconstruct the protection chain and explain why different erase operations serve different operational boundaries.

slides.title: Follow Every Layer Through Its Lifecycle
slides.subtitle: By the end of this course, you will be able to:
objectives: Build the protection hierarchy from the device root to an engine-ready MEK.
Distinguish fuse, durable-flash, and volatile key state.
Explain MPK and epoch transitions, including their reset behavior.
Compare double-wrapped random MEKs with derived MEKs.
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you'll be able to trace the L.O.C.K. key hierarchy without treating it as one undifferentiated key ladder.

You'll identify who supplies or controls each protection key and explain whether that value is durable, volatile, or ephemeral. You'll distinguish a Locked MPK from an Enabled MPK and explain why HPKE protects its access key in transit.

You'll follow the Hard and Soft Epoch Key lifecycle, including the fuse states and ordering rules that make zeroization meaningful. You'll then compare a randomly generated, double-wrapped Media Encryption Key with a deterministic derived key and its optional checksum.

Finally, you'll connect the hierarchy to operational choices. A soft epoch transition can support a tenant boundary. A hard epoch transition supports a device leaving its previous trust environment. Those choices make sense only after the relationships among the keys are clear.

slides.title: Each Layer Adds a Different Administrative Boundary
slides.subtitle: The final MEK secret is the ordered result of device, management, and epoch protection.

bullets.text: A DPK binds the hierarchy to a specific storage controller.
Zero or more ordered MPKs represent customer, fleet, or organizational boundaries.
An EPK combines hardware and software epoch material for the current environment.
The resulting MEK secret protects random or derived MEKs; an MDK secures the final device-local path.

figure.alt: Animation building the DPK, ordered MPKs, EPK, MEK secret, MDK, and engine key path layer by layer.
figure.caption: The hierarchy is ordered: changing any active parent changes access to the protected MEK state.

entries.text: “it’s just keys all the way down.”

slides.transcript:
The hierarchy is easier to understand when it is built from ownership toward the encryption engine.

Start with the Data Protection Key. The nominal owner of the data controls this value. In an Opal or Enterprise flow, drive firmware may recover it from a credential-protected structure. In Key Per I/O, it may be the imported data-encryption key associated with a key tag. One DPK binds to a given Media Encryption Key.

Next come zero or more Multi-party Protection Keys. Each MPK represents an additional authority that must assent before the media key can be loaded. The order matters because the KMB mixes the enabled MPKs into the secret one at a time. Using zero MPKs preserves compatibility with ordinary Opal, Enterprise, or Key Per I/O flows.

Then add the epoch layer. The Hard Epoch Key and Soft Epoch Key enter an SP 800-108 KDF to produce the Epoch Protection Key. The EPK, DPK, and configured MPKs produce the Media Encryption Key secret.

Finally, the Media Encryption Key Deobfuscation Key protects the hardware path used to place a random or derived media key into the Key Vault and then the encryption engine. It prevents compromised runtime firmware from turning a permitted decrypt operation into a key-disclosure path.

At the 2026 OCP EMEA Summit, Carl Lundin summarized the visual complexity with a memorable line: “it's just keys all the way down.” The engineering point is precise. Every layer has a different owner, lifetime, and failure consequence.

slides.title: Persistence Determines What a Reset Can—and Cannot—Change
slides.subtitle: Fuses establish roots, flash retains policy state, and volatile memory holds enabled working state.

bullets.text: Device secrets and 4 to 16 HEK slots survive resets and establish immutable hardware roots.
Locked MPKs, SEK state, counters, and wrapped objects persist in flash.
Enabled MPKs, VEK-protected working material, HPKE private state, and loaded MEKs live in protected runtime memory.
The KMB recreates device-local roots, establishes fresh HPKE state, and lazily creates a VEK when needed.

figure.alt: Matrix mapping fuse, durable flash, and volatile state to cold-reset behavior.
figure.caption: A reset policy is meaningful only when each key’s persistence class is explicit.

entries.text: Cold boot rebuilds device-local roots, creates fresh HPKE state, and generates the VEK lazily.

slides.transcript:
Durable, volatile, and ephemeral are not storage labels. They describe what an attacker can recover after a reset, power loss, or invasive analysis.

Durable values survive because they are stored in flash or fuses, or because they can be derived entirely from durable inputs. Locked MPKs and wrapped media keys are examples of ciphertext that drive firmware may retain. Hard Epoch Key seeds live in one-time-programmable fuses. The Soft Epoch Key may live in rewritable flash.

Volatile values live in protected memory and disappear on a cold reset or power cycle. HPKE private keys are generated at startup. The Volatile Escrow Key is created lazily, then protects Enabled MPKs held by drive firmware. Losing the VEK invalidates those enabled values without changing the durable Locked MPKs.

Ephemeral values exist only for the cryptographic operation that needs them. Plaintext access keys, Data Protection Keys, decrypted MPKs, and intermediate secrets are zeroized after use.

Caliptra's Key Vault gives the strongest hardware isolation. Slots sixteen through twenty-three are reserved for L.O.C.K.. They hold the MDK, EPK, VEK, Locked-MPK encryption keys, media-key secrets, the HEK, and the active Media Encryption Key in assigned slots.

Some sensitive values must temporarily exist in protected KMB memory because current Caliptra data paths don't support every required operation directly inside the Key Vault. That is a documented hardware constraint, not permission for drive firmware to see them. The security boundary still encloses KMB firmware, hardware engines, and Key Vault while excluding ordinary drive firmware.

slides.title: An MPK Moves from Locked Storage to Enabled Runtime State
slides.subtitle: HPKE grants access; the VEK protects the working copy.

bullets.text: An MPK can persist as a protected durable object without being usable for MEK operations.
Authorized HPKE material lets the KMB validate and recover the management layer.
The KMB keeps the active MPK inside protected volatile memory under the VEK.
Cold reset removes enabled working state; durable locked state can be enabled again after fresh authorization.

figure.alt: Animation showing a locked MPK being authorized through HPKE and protected by the VEK in enabled volatile state.
figure.caption: Locked is durable; Enabled is a protected runtime condition.

slides.transcript:
Multi-party protection turns one unlock credential into a set of required assents.

Each MPK begins with an external 256-bit access key. The user retrieves an HPKE public key and its certificate from the device, validates the certificate and DICE chain, checks the advertised algorithms, seals the access key, and sends it back. The host can carry that ciphertext without learning the access key.

During generation, the KMB unwraps the access key, creates a random MPK, and derives a wrapping key from the HEK, SEK, and access key. The returned Locked MPK can be stored durably by drive firmware.

Before that MPK can help load a media key, it must be enabled. The KMB unwraps the access key again, decrypts the Locked MPK, and re-encrypts the same key under the volatile VEK. Drive firmware may cache this Enabled MPK in memory. Because the VEK disappears on cold reset, the enabled form also becomes unusable.

Access-key rotation requires proof of both the old and new access keys. The KMB decrypts with the old binding, re-encrypts with the new one, and the drive zeroizes the old Locked MPK. Access-key testing uses a freshness nonce and returns an SHA-384 digest over metadata, the decrypted access key, and that nonce.

Version 1.1 advertises three KEM choices for this transport: P-384, ML-KEM-1024, and a hybrid that combines both. The hybrid option protects the same authorization flow with classical and post-quantum key establishment.

slides.title: Soft and Hard Epoch Changes Solve Different Operational Problems
slides.subtitle: Choose the transition according to whether the drive stays inside the trusted environment.

bullets.text: The active epoch combines a selected HEK fuse slot with durable SEK state.
Rotate the software-controlled epoch for an operational or tenant boundary while the hardware remains trusted.
Move to a different hardware epoch root before a drive leaves the environment or crosses a stronger ownership boundary.
Retiring an epoch removes the parent material needed to recover MEKs protected under that epoch.

figure.alt: Animation contrasting soft software-epoch rotation with a hard hardware-epoch transition.
figure.caption: A soft boundary rotates SEK state; a hard boundary moves to a different HEK root.

entries.text: one hardware root · one software-controlled epoch
The drive stays in the trusted environment. Rotate software epoch state for an operational or tenant boundary.
The drive leaves an environment or crosses a stronger ownership boundary. Move to a different fuse-rooted epoch.

slides.transcript:
The epoch keys turn erase into a state transition that the device can enforce.

The Soft Epoch Key is managed by drive firmware in rewritable storage. The Hard Epoch Key is derived inside Caliptra from a 256-bit fuse-held seed and device-identity material. Both must be available to derive the Epoch Protection Key. If either one is zeroized, existing media-key protection chains can no longer be reconstructed.

A device implements four to sixteen HEK fuse slots. The MCU moves each slot from blank to randomized to zeroized, and zeroizes it by blowing every bit. A shipped device must be in the production lifecycle with a randomized HEK seed.

Ordering matters. Firmware may program the SEK only while the HEK is available. It may zeroize the HEK seed only after the SEK is zeroized. It may enable permanent-HEK mode only after all HEK slots are zeroized. Pre-production and permanent modes can derive an HEK from an all-zero seed, but only under the lifecycle conditions defined by the specification.

After cold reset, MCU ROM must call report HEK metadata exactly once before Caliptra runtime firmware loads. If it does not, the KMB disables HEK-dependent operations.

The 2026 OCP EMEA Summit discussion gives the operational distinction. Rotate or zeroize the soft epoch key when data must be separated across tenant boundaries. Zeroize the hard epoch key when the physical device must be safe outside its former trust environment. If a failed controller can still complete and report that fuse transition, the drive can retain a meaningful erase claim. If it cannot, operators should not infer the same assurance.

slides.title: Random and Derived MEKs Reach the Same Protected Engine Boundary
slides.subtitle: Their creation and recovery paths differ, but plaintext key material stays inside the KMB.

bullets.text: A generated MEK is inner-wrapped with the MDK using AES-ECB, then outer-protected with the MEK secret using preconditioned AES-GCM.
A CMAC KDF combines an input seed with the MDK path to recreate key material when needed.
The random-key outer envelope authenticates its protected object; derived keys may include a 128-bit checksum.
Random keys preserve wrapped objects; derived keys trade storage for deterministic regeneration.

figure.alt: Split-path diagram comparing double-wrapped random MEKs with CMAC-KDF-derived MEKs.
figure.caption: Both paths terminate inside the KMB-to-engine protected transfer boundary.

slides.transcript:
Once the KMB has built the media-key secret, an integrator chooses one of two protected paths.

The random path begins with the DRBG. The KMB generates a 512-bit Media Encryption Key, then protects it twice. An inner AES-ECB layer uses the MDK. An outer preconditioned AES-GCM layer uses the media-key secret and carries the integrity tag. Drive firmware stores the double-wrapped result.

Later, the KMB removes the outer layer, routes the inner decryption through the MDK-controlled hardware path, and sends the plaintext key directly to the encryption engine.

The inner layer solves a subtle hardware problem. Without it, compromised KMB runtime firmware could misuse the AES engine's similar encrypt and decrypt paths to return a plaintext media key to firmware. Hardware forces an MDK-keyed ECB decryption result back into the Key Vault instead.

The derived path is deterministic. A CMAC-based SP 800-108 KDF produces a firmware-visible seed from the media-key secret because the available HMAC path would keep its result inside the Key Vault. The MDK path then converts that seed into the final media key.

An optional 128-bit checksum lets firmware detect whether later derivation from the same intended inputs would produce a different key, perhaps because a volatile SEK suffered a bit flip. A mismatch blocks programming and helps prevent unrecoverable data writes.

Both paths check the component-key inequality required for 256-bit and 512-bit AES-XTS use. Both finish with the same invariant: drive firmware never receives the plaintext Media Encryption Key.

slides.title: Every Layer Has a Purpose, Location, and Retirement Rule
items: The ordered hierarchy is DPK, zero or more MPKs, and an EPK before the MEK secret protects MEK state.
HEKs live in 4 to 16 fuse slots; SEK state supplies the software-controlled half of an epoch.
Locked MPKs persist, while Enabled MPKs are VEK-protected volatile working state.
Soft and hard epoch transitions represent different operational boundaries.
Random MEKs are double wrapped; derived MEKs are recreated through the device-local KDF path.
slides.transcript:
The L.O.C.K. hierarchy separates ownership, authorization, erase, and hardware-path protection.

One Data Protection Key represents the data owner. Zero or more ordered Multi-party Protection Keys add other authorities. Each MPK is durable in its Locked form and volatile in its Enabled form, where the VEK protects it. HPKE keeps the external access key confidential from the host.

The Hard and Soft Epoch Keys combine into the EPK. A soft transition supports a rewritable operational boundary. A hard fuse transition supports a stronger physical-device boundary. Either one can make the existing media-key chain unrecoverable.

The MDK constrains the final hardware path so compromised runtime firmware can't disclose a decrypted media key. Random Media Encryption Keys are double-wrapped. Derived keys follow a deterministic seed path and can use a checksum to detect input corruption.

Persistence is part of the security design. Durable ciphertext, volatile enablement, ephemeral plaintext, and hardware-isolated Key Vault values behave differently across reset and power loss. The final module turns those relationships into commands, registers, reset rules, and an integration checklist.

slides.title: Check the Key Hierarchy

DPK and VEK

choices.text: MPK and MDK

choices.text: HPKE public and private keys

questions.prompt: Which lifecycle statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

An Enabled MPK is protected in volatile KMB state
Cold reset clears enabled working state
A derived MEK must always be stored as a wrapped key object

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Durable locked state and volatile enabled state serve different parts of the lifecycle.

The first question checks which two keys combine to produce the Epoch Protection Key. The second asks you to distinguish the durable Locked MPK, the volatile Enabled MPK, and the Media Encryption Key itself.

slides.title: OCP L.O.C.K.
slides.subtitle: Controller Integration and Compliance
slides.transcript:
Module three. Integrating OCP L.O.C.K.: interfaces and compliance.

The key hierarchy protects data only when every request, reset, and error follows the intended path. Drive firmware talks to the Key Management Block through a mailbox. The KMB talks to the encryption engine through special function registers. A defined command sequence builds the media-key secret before a key can be generated, loaded, or derived.

This module maps those interfaces, then closes with the thirteen mandatory controls in version 1.1. By the end, you'll be able to review an integration flow for both functional order and security boundaries.

slides.title: Turn the Model into a Controller Contract
slides.subtitle: By the end of this course, you will be able to:
objectives: Separate the control mailbox from the protected MEK-transfer interface.
Read the MEK SFR layout and cache identity fields.
Sequence initialization, mixing, generation, load, derivation, and zeroization.
Map resets and the 13 mandatory behaviors to an integration checklist.
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you'll be able to separate the two implementation interfaces and explain why both are required.

You'll identify which data drive firmware can control, which values only the KMB can handle, and how the encryption engine stores each media key with metadata and auxiliary information.

You'll sequence the commands that initialize the media-key secret, mix zero or more MPKs, and then generate, load, or derive the final key. You'll also group the mailbox vocabulary by HPKE discovery, multi-party lifecycle, and media-key lifecycle instead of memorizing one long command list.

Finally, you'll connect TCG host operations to those services and evaluate reset, timeout, authorization, key-cache clearing, and KAT behavior against the mandatory compliance requirements. The goal is not to memorize every byte field. It is to know which ordering and ownership mistakes could expose a key, leave stale key material active, or cause permanent data loss.

slides.title: Commands and Key Transfer Use Different Interfaces
slides.subtitle: The separation keeps policy traffic flexible while constraining plaintext MEK movement.

bullets.text: A mailbox carries L.O.C.K. requests, identifiers, wrapped objects, status, and reports.
Dedicated SFRs carry up to 512 bits of MEK material, metadata, auxiliary data, and control.
Both paths terminate in the KMB, but ordinary firmware cannot read plaintext key transfer.
ENGINE_ID and SLOT_ID bind an operation to the intended encryption-engine location.

figure.alt: Animation showing mailbox traffic terminating at the Caliptra KMB and a separate protected SFR transfer carrying plaintext MEK material from the KMB to an explicitly selected encryption-engine slot.
figure.caption: Control is message-oriented; plaintext MEK transfer is register-bound and protected.

entries.text: PLAINTEXT MEK STAYS INSIDE THIS BOUNDARY

slides.transcript:
L.O.C.K. defines two interfaces because control policy and plaintext key transfer belong to different trust domains.

The mailbox interface connects drive firmware on the MCU to the Caliptra Key Management Block. Firmware uses it to discover HPKE capabilities, manage MPKs, initialize and extend a media-key secret, establish or unload media keys, query status, and clear the key cache. Inputs may include the Soft Epoch Key, a Data Protection Key, sealed access keys, encrypted MPKs, non-secret metadata, and timeouts.

The encryption-engine interface connects the KMB to the vendor's line-rate encryption hardware. It uses special function registers, or SFRs, to present a Media Encryption Key, its metadata, optional auxiliary data, and a control command. The raw media key crosses only this protected boundary. It is never returned through the mailbox.

Drive firmware still arbitrates the operation. It decides which host request is authorized, which metadata identifies the target key-cache entry, and when a key should load, unload, or be erased. But the KMB derives or unwraps the key and performs the protected transfer.

This division also creates an auditable failure boundary. A malformed mailbox request can fail before any engine operation. An engine that isn't ready produces an immediate not-ready result. A command that runs too long returns a timeout. An engine error is carried back with control-register context so firmware can surface it to the host without exposing the key.

The result is one protected key path with two narrowly defined control surfaces.

slides.title: The SFR Map Makes Key Transfer Explicit and Auditable
slides.subtitle: A compact register window couples key bytes, identity, optional data, and one command.

bullets.text: 64 bytes at the base address carry up to 512 bits of key material.
20 bytes at base plus 0x40 identify engine, slot, key length, and cache context.
32 bytes at base plus 0x60 carry command-specific auxiliary data.
The register at base plus 0x80 selects Load, Unload, Zeroize, or optional KAT behavior.

figure.alt: Register map showing the 64-byte MEK, 20-byte metadata, 32-byte AUX, and CTRL regions plus engine and slot identity.
figure.caption: The SFR contract binds a key operation to explicit engine, slot, length, and control fields.

slides.transcript:
The encryption engine stores a tuple, not a bare key.

Each key-cache entry contains non-secret metadata, optional auxiliary data, and a 512-bit Media Encryption Key. Metadata identifies the entry. A vendor might use a namespace plus an LBA range, or a namespace plus a Key Per I/O tag. Auxiliary data can select a mode or carry an initialization-vector offset. Neither field may create a path for reading the media key.

The SFR layout makes that tuple explicit. The 64-byte media-key register begins at the configured base address. The 20-byte metadata region begins at base + 0x40. The 32-byte aux region begins at base + 0x60. The control register sits at base + 0x80. MCU ROM configures and locks the base and length before runtime firmware can modify them.

The control command selects four actions. Command one loads a media key. Command two unloads the entry identified by metadata. Command three zeroizes the entire key cache. Optional command four loads a fixed Known Answer Test key for FIPS validation.

That test key requires a strict warning. It has a published pattern chosen to avoid endianness ambiguity and satisfy AES-XTS component-key inequality. It is not secret and must never encrypt user data. After the test, firmware must unload it or clear the entire cache.

The control handshake uses ready, command, execute, done, and error fields. The KMB checks ready, writes the command and execute bit, waits for done, reads the error, acknowledges done, and waits for the engine to return to its idle state.

slides.title: Every MEK Operation Begins with an Explicit Secret Context
slides.subtitle: Initialization and ordered mixing precede generation, load, or derivation.

bullets.text: INITIALIZE_MEK_SECRET starts a fresh operation context from the active hierarchy.
Zero or more MIX_MEK_SECRET operations add ordered context before a final key action.
Generate or load a random MEK object, or derive a MEK from supplied seed material.
The KMB loads the selected engine slot; unload and zeroize commands remove usable runtime state.

figure.alt: Animation showing initialization, optional ordered MPK mixing, and exactly one final action: generate a wrapped random key, load a random key into an engine slot, or derive and load a key into an engine slot.
figure.caption: The state machine prevents a final MEK action from occurring outside an initialized hierarchy context.

entries.text: ONE INITIALIZED CONTEXT → ONE FINAL ACTION
discard the partial context after success or error

slides.transcript:
Establishing a media key is a short stateful choreography. The order protects both correctness and secrecy.

Every path starts with initialize MEK secret. Drive firmware supplies the Soft Epoch Key and Data Protection Key. Inside the KMB, the HEK and SEK produce the Epoch Protection Key, and the EPK combines with the DPK to create the initial media-key-secret seed.

Firmware may then invoke mix MPK zero or more times. Each call supplies one Enabled MPK. The KMB decrypts it under the VEK and extends the secret seed through a key derivation function. The order must match the order associated with that Media Encryption Key. Calling mix before initialization is an error.

The path then branches.

For a new random key, firmware calls generate MEK. The KMB creates a 512-bit key and returns only the protected Wrapped MEK. When the drive later needs that key, it repeats initialization and the same MPK sequence, then calls load MEK with metadata, auxiliary data, the wrapped key, and a timeout. The KMB unwraps and sends the key to the engine.

For a deterministic key, firmware repeats the same initialization and mixing, then calls derive MEK. It may include the stored checksum from an earlier derivation. A mismatch blocks the load.

Initialization is single-use state for an establishment attempt. Integrators should treat each command sequence as a transaction: build the secret from the intended inputs, establish exactly one key, handle errors, and never reuse a partially constructed chain for a different key.

slides.title: Map Product APIs to Five L.O.C.K. Operation Families
slides.subtitle: The host-facing command set may vary, but the security semantics must remain visible.

bullets.text: Report capabilities, supported algorithms, HEK metadata, limits, and current state.
Provision or authorize management layers and construct the active MEK-secret context.
Generate, import, derive, load, unload, and zeroize MEKs for explicit engine slots.
Rotate epochs, handle reset boundaries, report measurements, and expose compliance-relevant evidence.

figure.alt: Five grouped host API families for discovery, management layers, MEK operations, epoch transitions, and evidence.
figure.caption: A product can choose its transport while preserving the L.O.C.K. operation semantics.

slides.transcript:
Host protocols expose user intent. The mailbox translates that intent into a smaller protected vocabulary.

Start with HPKE discovery. Firmware asks the KMB for supported algorithms and active handles, retrieves each public key, and uses its MCU DPE context to endorse that key. A host can then validate the certificate chain before sealing an access key. Rotating a certificate-table entry maps to rotating the underlying HPKE keypair.

The MPK lifecycle maps to the TCG Media Encryption Key Multiparty Authorization feature. Initializing an access condition generates a Locked MPK. Changing its access key rewraps it. Enabling the access condition produces an Enabled MPK. Testing the key returns the nonce-bound digest. Binding an encryption-key entry to that access condition becomes a mix MPK operation during media-key establishment.

Ordinary TCG Opal and Enterprise flows may generate, load, or derive media keys with zero MPKs. Key Per I/O uses derive MEK when an imported data-encryption key and key tag become the DPK and metadata inputs.

The 2026 OCP EMEA Summit update explained why standards work and implementation work had to advance together. The group contributed across Caliptra, TCG, and NIST-facing requirements. Implementation feedback also simplified the version 1.1 key ladder by replacing an earlier bespoke key-combination construct with the standard SP 800-108 KDF.

That is the integration lesson: stable host semantics, narrow protected commands, and standard cryptographic building blocks reduce the amount of security-sensitive custom behavior each vendor must invent.

slides.title: Reset Semantics Are Part of the Security Contract
slides.subtitle: Conformance requires both correct cryptography and correct state transitions.

bullets.text: Derive HEK and MDK state, create fresh HPKE state, and generate a VEK lazily when volatile MPK protection is first needed.
Preserve HEK, MDK, and VEK state while regenerating HPKE state.
Preserve the same device-local and volatile protection roots while rotating HPKE access state.
Table 56 defines 13 required behaviors covering hardware roots, reporting order, protected transfer, algorithms, lifecycle, and zeroization.

figure.alt: Matrix comparing cold reset, warm reset, firmware update, and the mandatory compliance baseline.
figure.caption: A compliant implementation must preserve or recreate each key class exactly as the reset model specifies.

entries.text: Roots · reporting order · algorithms · protected transfer · lifecycle · zeroization

slides.transcript:
Reset behavior determines which protected state remains valid.

On cold reset, Caliptra ROM derives the HEK and MDK. Runtime firmware determines whether an HEK is available and generates fresh HPKE keypairs for every supported algorithm. The VEK is not created until first use. A Caliptra cold reset occurs only with an NVMe subsystem reset caused by main power being applied.

On warm or firmware-update reset, the HEK, MDK, and VEK remain. HPKE keypairs do not. Firmware must re-enumerate and advertise the regenerated handles when it supports a host-facing API. Other integration reset events may map to a Caliptra warm reset.

Those state rules sit inside thirteen mandatory requirements. The device must integrate and enable L.O.C.K.. In production, only Caliptra may program Media Encryption Keys. Power loss or device zeroization must remove every key from the engine. A shipped device must be in production with a randomized HEK.

MCU ROM must populate the HEK seed register and call report HEK metadata after cold reset. HEK and SEK values must be cryptographically strong. Drive firmware must authorize destructive lifecycle events. The KMB must reach the defined SFRs at the immutable configured address and length. Integrations must follow the reset directives.

Finally, the optional fixed KAT media key must never encrypt user data.

Use Table fifty-six in the specification as the definitive checklist, not this summary. Then use an OCP S.A.F.E. review to verify that the product's actual firmware, register protections, resets, and engine behavior preserve the intended trust boundary.

slides.title: Integrate the Boundary, Not Just the Algorithms
items: Mailbox commands and protected MEK-transfer SFRs are separate interfaces with different exposure rules.
The 64-byte MEK, 20-byte metadata, 32-byte AUX, and CTRL regions make engine programming explicit.
Initialize and optional ordered mixing occur before random-key or derived-key final actions.
Host transports may differ, but capability, lifecycle, key, epoch, and evidence semantics must remain intact.
Cold reset, warm reset, firmware update, and the 13 mandatory requirements are all part of conformance.
slides.transcript:
A conformant L.O.C.K. integration preserves one plaintext key path while exposing two control interfaces.

Drive firmware uses the mailbox to request protected services. The KMB uses SFRs to load, unload, or zeroize encryption-engine entries. Metadata and auxiliary data remain vendor-defined, but neither may expose the raw Media Encryption Key.

Media-key establishment always starts by initializing the secret. Zero or more ordered mix MPK calls extend it. The sequence then branches to random-key generation and loading, or deterministic derivation.

Host protocols map onto grouped services for HPKE discovery, MPK lifecycle, and media-key lifecycle. Implementation feedback in version 1.1 reduced bespoke cryptography and aligned these services with Caliptra and TCG mechanisms.

Reset rules decide which keys persist and which handles must be rediscovered. Authorization, timeouts, engine errors, immutable register configuration, cache clearing, and safe KAT handling are security requirements, not operational polish.

Use the specification's thirteen mandatory controls as the checklist and OCP S.A.F.E. review as the integration verification step. That closes the path from threat model, through key hierarchy, to an auditable product implementation.

questions.prompt: Which statements belong to a compliant integration? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Plaintext MEKs transfer through the protected SFR path
ENGINE_ID and SLOT_ID bind an operation to a target

Ordinary firmware may read the MEK region for diagnostics

This final check focuses on integration order and mandatory behavior.

The first question asks which command must initialize the media-key secret before any MPK can be mixed or any key established. The second asks you to select required behaviors across power loss, reset, authorization, register setup, and KAT handling.

Submit both questions once to continue. Correct answers aren't required, and retry feedback is available. Use the feedback to distinguish flexible vendor metadata from security controls that every conformant integration must preserve.
